en: Laziness and fickleness—through these six, yoga is destroyed. || 15 ||
Through enthusiasm, daring, fortitude, and certainty born from the knowledge of reality, and through the renunciation of association with worldly people—by these six, yoga is perfected. (16)
I shall describe some of the postures adopted by sages such as Vasiṣṭha and others, as well as by yogis such as Matsyendra and others. (17)
Having first attained the initial stage of Haṭha, the Āsana is taught;
one should practice that, for it brings stability of posture, health, and lightness of the limbs. (18)
Having properly placed both soles of the feet between the knees and the thighs, one should sit with the body straight; that is called the Svastika posture.
One should place the right ankle on the left side of the back, and likewise the left ankle on the right; this is the *gomukha* posture, just like the face of a cow.
Placing one foot upon one thigh and likewise the other thigh upon the second [foot], this is declared to be the vīrāsana posture. || 21 ||
Having bound the ankles with the feet in reverse order while remaining composed, this becomes the tortoise posture (kūrmāsana); so the knowers of yoga understand.

Having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana) by placing the hands between the knees and the thighs, and having established them on the ground, one remains suspended in the air; this is the cock posture (kukkuṭāsana).
Seated in the cock-posture (kukkuṭāsana), with the neck held steady by both arms, one should lie on one's back like a tortoise;
this is the "upward-tortoise" (uttānakūrmaka) posture.
Having grasped the two big toes with both hands up to the ears and drawing the bow, this is declared to be the Dhanurāsana (the Bow Posture). || 25 ||

With the right foot placed at the root of the left thigh and the right arm encircling the thighs from the outside, one stands with the body turned; this shall be the posture declared by the illustrious Matsyanātha. (26)
The Matsyendrapīṭha is a weapon that shatters the fierce solar orb (ruṇmaṇḍala) trembling within the belly;
by practicing it, one awakens the Kuṇḍalinī and bestows steadiness like a staff upon men.
Extending the two feet on the ground in the form of a staff and grasping the pair of feet with both arms—
With the forehead resting upon the knees, one should enter; this is not said to be the western direction. || 28 ||
Thus, by means of the western [channel], one does not make the foremost wind flow through the western vehicle;
rather, it acts upon the stomach and the digestive fire of the belly, producing leanness in the abdomen and freedom from disease for men. (29)
Supporting the earth with both palms, with the sides of the abdomen resting upon the elbows,
and rising from a high seat like a staff— this they call the Khemāyūra posture.

The venerable Mayūra-āsana swiftly removes all diseases such as abdominal tumors and enlargement; it overcomes the humors (doṣas), turns even a large quantity of food into ash, generates the digestive fire in its entirety, and can digest even the Kālakūṭa poison. || 31 ||
Lying on the ground like a corpse on its back is the corpse posture (śavāsana);
it removes confusion regarding all postures and is the means for achieving mental clarity. || 32 ||
Eighty-four types of seats have indeed been described by Śiva;
taking from among them a quartet that constitutes the essence, I shall now speak of them.
The fourfold [postures]—Siddha, Padma, Bhadra, and Siṃha—are excellent;
among them, O friend, always remain in the Siddhāsana.
The Siddhāsana posture.
Having firmly joined the soles of the feet at the root of the perineum,
one should place one foot upon the penis; holding this posture in the heart,
with the body like a pillar and the senses restrained, one should gaze with a steady eye at the space between the eyebrows— this is the very bolt for the door of liberation.
That which produces differentiation is called Siddhāsana. || 35 ||
In another opinion:
Having placed the left ankle below the penis and upon that [right thigh], and having inserted the space between the ankles [under the other thigh], this becomes Siddhāsana. || 36 ||
Matsyendra calls this very posture *stana*; others know it as *siddhāsana*, while others understand it as *vajrāsana*.
Some call it *muktāprāṇa*, and others call it *guptāsana*. (37)
Among the restraints (yamas), moderation in food is thus supreme; among the observances (niyamas), non-violence is likewise so.
Among all postures, the perfected ones know Siddhāsana to be the one that is foremost. (38)
One should constantly practice that which is already perfected within the eighty-four *pīṭhas*, just as one [focuses] upon the *suṣumṇā* among the seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍīs*). 39.
Meditating on the Self and restricting one's diet for as long as twelve years, through the constant practice of *siddhāsana* and other methods, one shall attain the state of a Yoginī. (40)
When the Siddhāsana is attained, what is the use of many laborious postures?
For when the vital breath (prāṇānila) is firmly bound through simple Kumbhaka with full attention, [all is achieved]. (41)
The state of Unmanī arises effortlessly and spontaneously of its own accord, once one is always firmly established in the Siddhāsana alone. 42.
The three bandhas arise spontaneously and without effort.
There is no posture equal to that of the Siddhas, no kumbhaka like Kevala-yama, no mudrā equal to Khecarī, and no dissolution (laya) like that of Nāda. (43)
Now, the lotus posture (padmāsana).
Placing the right foot upon the left thigh and likewise the left foot upon the right thigh,
holding them firmly with both hands according to the posterior method,
placing the thumbs at the heart, and resting the chin [there], one should gaze at the tip of the nose; this is Vyādhi-bandha.
The lotus posture (padmāsana) is said to be the destroyer of these [afflictions]. || 44 ||
But according to another opinion:
Having carefully placed the two feet flat upon the thighs,
one should then place the two hands firmly between the thighs with their palms facing upward.
O King, one should place the tip of the tongue at the root of the teeth;
holding the chin up and pressing it against the chest, one should slowly draw in the breath.
This is declared to be the lotus posture (padmāsana), which destroys all diseases;
it is difficult for anyone to attain, yet it is obtained on earth by the wise.
Afterwards, the *Matsyendramata* was spoken.
Having joined the hands firmly together, assume the lotus posture (padmāsana);
place the chin firmly against the chest, and fix that meditation within your mind.

By repeatedly drawing up the downward-moving breath (apāna) into the upward path, filling it, and releasing the vital breath (prāṇa), one attains incomparable awakening through the power of this capacity. || 48 ||
The yogi, seated in the lotus posture, should fill [the breath] through the openings of the channels;
he who restrains the vital air is liberated—of this there is no doubt. (49)
Now, the lion throne.
One should place the two ankles below the penis and on either side of the perineum;
the right ankle on the left [side] and the left ankle on the right.
34a) Having placed the two hands upon the knees and having fully extended the fingers,
one should gaze with an open mouth at the tip of the nose, being well-composed.
This lion-throne (siṃhāsana) is always honored by yogis;
it effects the joining of the bonds and is the best of postures.
Now, the auspicious posture (bhadrāsana).
One should place the two ankles below the scrotum on both sides of the perineal seam;
then, having firmly bound the sides of the feet with the hands, [the body] should be made perfectly motionless.
This Bhadrāsana destroys all diseases;
indeed, the Siddha-yogins call this Gorakṣāsana. (54)
Thus, when the postures have been mastered, the lord of yogis, having overcome fatigue,
should then practice the purification of the channels (nāḍī-śuddhi), the mudrās, and the exercises for the vital breath (pavana-kriyā).
Posture, diverse breath control (kumbhaka), the adoption of mudrās, and then the contemplation of sound (nāda)—this is the sequence of practice in Haṭha Yoga. (56)
A practitioner of yoga who observes celibacy, eats moderately, and is devoted to yoga shall become a perfected one after a year; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. || 57 ||
That which is eaten for the sake of pleasing Śiva— consisting of very smooth and sweet food, with one-fourth of the stomach left empty— is called "moderate diet" (mitāhāra).

They say that for one on a low path, it is unwholesome to consume pungent, sour, bitter, salty, or hot foods; leafy vegetables, fermented gruel, oil, sesame, mustard, fish, meat from goats and other animals, curd, buttermilk, *kulattha* beans, *kola*, *pippalī*, asafoetida, and garlic.

One should know that food which is unwholesome is that which is parched, dry, excessively salty, containing fermented liquors (āsava), meat, pungent condiments, vegetables, and an abundance of flour-based preparations. (60)
One should avoid friendship with the wicked, as well as service to fire, women, and the path; likewise, one should avoid bodily mortifications such as bathing at dawn and fasting.

O Lord of Yamas, wheat, rice, barley, ṣaṣṭika rice, and other excellent grains; milk, clarified butter, sugar-candy, fresh butter, white sugar, and honey; ginger, the fruit of the *phaṭola*, and the five types of vegetables; mung beans and other pulses; and products of the cow—these are declared as fit for consumption.
Wholesome. || 62 ||
The yogi should partake of food that is sweet, very delicious, unctuous, derived from cow products, nourishing to the bodily constituents, desired by the mind, and suitable. 63.
Whether young or old, or even if aged, diseased, or weak,
one who is untiring in all yogic practices attains perfection through constant practice.
The seats (pīṭhas), the various breath-retentions (kuṃbhakas), and the divine postures (karaṇas)—all this practice of Haṭha Yoga has as its ultimate fruit Rājayoga. (65)
Thus ends the first instruction, titled "The Teaching on Restraints, Observances, and Postures," in the *Haṭhapradīpikā* composed by the lord of yogis, Svātmārāma.
Then, on a firm seat, the yogi, having subdued his appetite, should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) according to the path taught by the guru. || 1 ||
When the breath moves, everything moves; likewise, when it is still, everything is still.
The yogi attains the state of a pillar (immobility); therefore, he should restrain the vital air.
O Goddess, as long as the vital breath lives, how can knowledge arise in the mind? The mind does not die as long as the vital breath lives.
One who brings both the vital breath and the mind to dissolution attains liberation; no other person attains it by any means whatsoever. (3)
As long as the vital air remains steady within the body, so long is it said to be life;
death is its departure from the body, therefore one should restrain that air.

When the channels are congested with impurities, the vital wind does not move through the central channel; how then could the state of *unmanī* arise, and how could the perfection of the body be attained? (5)
When the entire network of channels (nāḍīcakra) is perceived by the intellect to be filled with impurities,
at that very moment the yogi becomes capable of restraining the vital breath (prāṇa).
Thereafter, one should daily practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) with a pure and sattvic mind,
so that all impurities residing within the suṣumṇā channel are completely eliminated.

The yogi, seated upon a lotus or a non-lotus seat, should fill his breath with the moon (the left nostril) according to his capacity; having retained it, he should exhale again through the sun (the right nostril).
Having performed the breath-retention (kuṃbhaka) according to the rules, one should again exhale through the moon (the left nostril).
35a) One should first retain that by which one would exhale, without cessation; and thereafter,
one should exhale from that very same place slowly, not with force.
If one should drink the breath through the iḍā, restrained, and then exhale it again through the other;
having drunk the wind through the piṅgalā, one should then hold it and release it through the left (iḍā).
By practicing according to this method for the sun and the moon,
the channels of the self-restrained become purified after three months.
One should practice eighty *kumbhakas* four times a day— at dawn, midday, evening, and midnight— gradually increasing until reaching that number.
In the lowest stage there is perspiration; in the middling stage, trembling occurs;
in the highest stage of breath-restraint, one rises up repeatedly while in the lotus posture.
One should perform a massage of the body with water produced from physical exertion;
through that, whether copious or slight, firmness of the body arises.
At the time of initial practice, a diet of milk and ghee is recommended;
thereafter, once the practice has become firm, one should likewise observe the formal rules of discipline.
Just as a lion, an elephant, or a tiger becomes submissive gradually and slowly, so too is the wind mastered when practiced correctly; otherwise, it destroys the practitioner.
Through the proper practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), there shall be the destruction of all diseases;
through improper practice of yoga, there arises the emergence of all diseases. || 16 ||
Hiccups, dyspnea, cough, and pain in the head, ears, and eyes—various disorders arise from the derangement of the wind (vāyu). || 17 ||
One should exhale the breath properly, fill it properly, and bind it properly;
in this way, one shall attain purity. || 18 ||
But when the purification of the channels occurs, then external signs certainly arise in the body: leanness and a radiant luster. (19)
From the purification of the channels, there arises the ability to retain the breath as desired, the kindling of the internal fire, the manifestation of the inner sound (nāda), and good health. (20)
One whose constitution is filled with fat, phlegm, and so forth, should perform the six purificatory acts (ṣaṭkarman);
however, another whose humors (doṣas) are in equilibrium should not perform them. (35b–21)
Dhauti, vasti, naiti, trāṭaka, naulikā,
and kapālabhāti— these are declared to be the six karmas.
This sixfold ritual action has been proclaimed as that which effects the purification of the vessel;
it bestows manifold virtues and should be honored with hymns by the foremost of men. (23)
Among those, dhauti is as follows:
One should swallow a cloth four finger-breadths wide using the corners of the mouth;
then one should draw it back out again—this is declared to be the practice of *dhauti*.
Cough, asthma, splenic enlargement, leprosy, and twenty types of phlegm diseases—by the power of the dhauti practice, these surely vanish; of this there is no doubt. (25)
Now, the enema (vasti).
With his seat firmly placed upon a vessel submerged in water reaching up to the navel,
the practitioner of the *basti* procedure should perform the contraction of the base (*ādhāra*) for the purpose of cleansing.

Furthermore, abdominal tumors, splenic enlargement, dropsy, and diseases arising from wind, bile, and phlegm, along with their various complications, are warded off by the power of the enema treatment.
The practice of the water enema (jalavasti) bestows joy upon the elements, the sense organs, and the internal organs, as well as luster and a blazing radiance;
it destroys the accumulation of all defects when practiced regularly.
Having raised the downward-moving wind (apāna) from the abdomen— purified by the mantra of the object within— along the channel of the throat,
those who know Haṭha call this "the elephant's trunk" (gajakaraṇī), as it brings the pathways of the wind under control through the power of gradual practice.
Then, one should insert a well-lubricated thread, one span in length, into the nasal passage;
one should cause it to emerge from the mouth—this is called *anīti* by the perfected ones (*siddhas*). (29)
The purifier of the skull, the bestower of divine vision upon the throat, the virtuous Satī quickly destroys the flood of diseases arising above the knees for those who bow to her on this earth. (30)
Now, the practice of *trāṭaka*.
With a steady gaze and a concentrated mind, one should look at a subtle object until tears begin to fall; this is known as Trāṭaka by the teachers.
Trāṭaka is a great pill for eye diseases and a bolt against drowsiness and other ailments;
it should be guarded with effort, like a casket of gold.
Now, the *nauli*.
With the force of a continuous whirlpool, one should rotate the belly from left to right and right to left;
with shoulders bent, this is revealed by the masters of the Daiva, Auliga, and Gauḍa traditions. (33)
This Nauli, the crest-jewel of Haṭha practices, always kindles a weak digestive fire, performs digestion and other functions, bestows bliss,
and dries up all defects and diseases.
Now follows the Kapālabhāti.
Like the bellows of a blacksmith, it involves rapid inhalation and exhalation;
this renowned practice, known as Kapālabhāti, dries up the disorder of phlegm (kapha). (35)
One should eliminate the excess phlegm, fat, and impurities produced by the six activities;
thereafter, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma), for it is accomplished without effort.
"By means of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) alone, the impurities are thoroughly subdued;
therefore, some teachers do not approve of any other practice. (37)
Even the thirty gods, beginning with Brahmā, became intent on the practice of breath-control (pavana) out of fear of Death; therefore, one should practice breath-control.
Even one afflicted by many diseases does not suffer if he is devoted to the practice of breath control;
for one who possesses a controlled mind, there is no fear of death. Therefore, one should practice breath control.
As long as the vital breath (marut) is bound within the body, so long the mind remains without support;
as long as [the breath] is held between the eyebrows, whence can there be fear of death? (41)
When the wheel of channels (nāḍī-cakra) has been purified according to rule by means of the unions of the vital breaths (prāṇa-saṃpāka),
the vital air (māruta) pierces the opening of the Suṣumṇā and enters through its mouth.
When the vital breath moves through the middle channel, steadiness of mind arises;
that state in which the mind becomes perfectly steady is this very condition known as *manonmanī*.
To achieve that, one who knows the method should perform various *kuṃbhakas*;
through the practice of diverse *kuṃbhakas*, one shall attain manifold accomplishments (*siddhi*). || 44 ||
Sūryabheda, Ujjāyī, Sītkārī, Śītalī, Bhastrikā,
Bhramarī, Mūrchā, and Kevala are the eight types of Kumbhaka.
At the end of inhalation (pūraka), the bind known as Jālandhara should be performed;
at the end of retention (kumbhaka) and at the beginning of exhalation (recaka), the Mūdrīyāṇaka should be performed.

By means of contraction, the foundation [of the breath] is quickly secured; when the constriction of the throat is performed, through the backward tension in the middle, that which resides in the Brahma-nāḍī shall be attained. (47)
36b) Having raised the *apāna* upward and led the *prāṇa* down from the throat,
the yogi, liberated from old age, shall become sixteen years of age.
Therein is the piercing of the sun.
Then, having assumed the vajrāsana posture on a comfortable seat, the yogi should slowly draw in the external breath through the right nāḍī. (49)
One should perform kumbhaka (retention) from the hair to the tips of the nails, until the cessation [of breath];
then, one should slowly exhale the air through the left nostril.
The purification of the skull destroys wind disorders and removes the defects caused by worms;
this should be performed again and again, and it is most excellent when done during the division of the sun.
Then follows the *ujjāyī*.
Restraining the mouth, one should slowly draw the dark wind through the channel so that it reaches from the throat down to the heart with a sound.
Then, as before, one should exhale the breath through the *iḍā* like a jar;
this removes the defects of phlegm and increases the digestive fire of the body. (53)
The kuṃbhaka known as ujjāpī should be performed by those who are walking, for it destroys the defects located in the channels, water, and the bodily constituents. || 54 ||
Now follows the practice of Sītkārī.
One should always apply a kiss to the mouth and a yawn to the nostrils;
through such practice of yoga, one becomes a second Kāmadeva. (55)
He is the common cause of creation and dissolution within the circle of Yoginīs;
neither hunger nor thirst, nor sleep nor even laziness arises [for him]. (56)
By this method, the lord of yogis shall constantly possess a body that is self-willed and free from all afflictions upon the surface of the earth. 57.

Thus it was said by Gorakṣa: "He who constantly drinks the vital breath (prāṇa) with the tongue against the root of the palate shall experience the destruction of all diseases above the age of eighty. (58)
Now follows Śītalī.
Having drawn in the air through the tongue as before, following the retention (kumbhaka),
one should slowly exhale the breath through both nostrils with focused awareness.
The breath-control known as *viṣāṇī* and *śītalī* destroys disorders such as abdominal tumors and splenic enlargement, as well as fever, bile, hunger, thirst, and poison. (60)
Now, the bellows.
When one places both hands upon the two thighs and the soles of the feet [rest upon the thighs],
that is the perfect Padmāsana, which destroys all evil.
Having properly assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), with neck and abdomen held straight, the wise practitioner should carefully control the mouth and exhale the breath through the nostril.
Then, as it touches the heart, throat, and cheeks with sound,
one should forcefully fill the air slightly as far as the heart.
One should purge again in that same manner and fill [the body] again and again, just as the bellows of smiths are blown by the force of their movement. (64)
Just as the abdomen becomes full [with air], one should hold it light with the wind;
one should hold the nose firmly with the middle fingers, excluding the index fingers.
Having performed the retention (kumbhaka) as before, one should exhale the breath through the iḍā;
this removes wind, bile, and phlegm, and increases the digestive fire of the body. (67)
The awakening of Kuṇḍalinī destroys all defects, bestows happiness, and is auspicious;
it removes the obstructions of phlegm and other humors situated within the opening of the Brahma-nāḍī.
This breath-retention known as *bhastrā* should especially be performed; it arises from the three qualities (*guṇas*) and pierces the three knots. (69)
Now, the *bhramarī* [mudrā].
With the *pūraka* [breath] having the sound of a rushing current and the humming of bees, and the *recaka* with the very gentle sound of a female bee—
through such practice of yoga by the lords of yogis, a certain swoon of bliss arises in the mind. (70)
Now, fainting.
At the end of the inhalation (pūraka), having firmly closed the nostrils (jālāndhara), one should slowly exhale;
this is called murchhanā, which bestows the bliss of mental absorption (manomūrchā).
With his inner breath set in motion and his belly filled by it,
he floats with ease even upon fathomless water like a lotus leaf.
Now follows the kevalakumbhaka (the complete breath-retention).

Prāṇāyāma is declared to be threefold by means of exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kuṃbhaka). Retention (kuṃbhaka) is considered to be of two kinds: sahita (accompanied) and kevala (unaccompanied). || 73 ||
Exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka) should be performed slowly and with coordination;
one should practice in this manner until the mastery of kevala-kumbhaka is attained.
Having abandoned both exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka), the comfortable retention of the vital air (vāyu) which is practiced as breath control (prāṇāyāma)—
that indeed is called pure kumbhaka.
When kevala kumbhaka is perfected—devoid of both exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka)—there is nothing whatsoever difficult to attain for him within the three worlds. (76)
One who is capable of retaining the breath at will using only the *kumbha* [breath-retention] attains perfectly the state of *rājayoga*; of this there is no doubt. (77)
Without Haṭha there is no Rājayoga, and without Rājayoga there is no Haṭha;
they do not succeed [individually]. Therefore, one should practice the pair until liberation is attained. (78)
At the end of the exhalation of the breath, one should perform the retention (kumbhaka) which makes the mind free from affliction;
through such practice of yoga, one shall attain the state of Rājayoga.
From kumbhaka comes the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī;
from the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī, the Suṣumnā becomes unobstructed and the perfection of Haṭha is born.

Emaciation of the body, brightness in the face, clarity of the channels, purity of the eyes, freedom from disease, mastery over the bindu, and longevity—these shall arise when the kumbhaka is performed here in the Kṛta age. (81)
Thus ends the second instruction, titled "The Characteristics of Prāṇāyāma with Variegated Kumbhakas," in the Haṭhapradīpikā composed by Ātmārāma Yogīndra.
Just as the mountain, the forest, and the nurse are the support for [the child], so indeed is the leader;
likewise, Kuṇḍalī is the foundation for all the Yoga Tantras.
By the grace of that sleeping Guru, by whom Kuṇḍalinī is awakened,
then all the lotuses and even the knots are pierced.
The state of emptiness of the vital breath acts as a royal highway, since the mind becomes supportless; thus is there the deception of time. (3)
Therefore, with every effort, one should practice the exercise of the mudrās upon the face of the Brahma-door, in order to awaken the Goddess who is sleeping there. (4)
Mahāmudrā-bandha, Mahāvedha, Khecarī, Ūḍīyāṇa, Mūlabandha, Jālandhara-bandha, and the one called Dharābandha. || 5 ||
Karaṇī, the one called Viparītā, Vajrolī, and Śakticālana—
this indeed is the group of ten mudrās that destroys old age and death.
38a) This [teaching], correctly proclaimed by the Primordial Lord (Ādinātha), bestows the eightfold sovereign powers;
it is beloved by all the Siddhas and difficult even for the gods to attain.
It must be guarded with great effort, like a casket of jewels; it must never be told to anyone, just as the amorous dalliance of a woman of noble family is kept secret.
Therein is Mahāmudrā.
Having firmly pressed the perineum with the left foot,
one should extend the right leg and hold it steady with both hands.
Having applied the binding at the throat, one should hold the breath upwards;
just as a snake struck by a staff becomes straight like a staff.
When the Kuṇḍalinī power suddenly becomes straightened,
then that state of death arises, residing in the two openings.
Then one should exhale very slowly indeed, and not with force;
this is truly the Mahāmudrā, which is praised by the great adepts (mahāsiddhas). || 12 ||
The defects such as birth, death, and so forth, which arise from great afflictions, are overcome;
yet even those supreme among the wise do not speak of Mahāmudrā to you. (13)
Having practiced on the lunar limb, one should practice again on the solar limb;
when the count has become equal, then one should release the mudrā.
Indeed, whether seeing or not seeing, all tastes are tasteless;
yet even that which has been consumed is digested like nectar.
For one who practices Mahāmudrā, diseases such as consumption, leprosy, colic, abdominal tumors, and splenic disorders go to their destruction. (16)
That which has been described as Mahāmudrā brings about great accomplishment for human beings; it must be guarded with effort and should not be given to just anyone. (17)
Now follows the Mahābandha (the great lock).
One should place the heel of the left foot in the region of the pubic organ,
and likewise place the right foot upon the left thigh.
Then, having filled the wind (prāṇa) and firmly pressing the pubic region against the heart, one should squeeze the yoni and, contracting [the body], join the mind within the navel. || 19 ||
Having retained [the breath] according to one's capacity, one should exhale the air slowly;
having practiced on the left side, one should practice again on the right side. 38b) 20.
In this regard, some hold the opinion that one should avoid [the food] stuck to the throat;
for it may be swallowed by the tongue between the two upper front teeth.
This indeed is the great bond that bestows great accomplishment;
it is the expert in liberation from the great bond of the noose of time. || 22 ||
But this [channel], awakening the upward movement of all the channels,
maintains the confluence of the triple stream (triveṇī) and leads the mind to Kedāra.
Just as a woman endowed with beauty and grace is [fruitless] without a man, so too the Mahāmudrā and the Mahābandha are fruitless when devoid of the prescribed ritual. (25)
Now, the Great Piercing (Mahāvedha).

Established in the great lock (mahābandha), the yogi of single-minded intellect, having performed the inhalation (pūraka) and having restrained the movement of the vital airs by means of the throat-lock (kaṇṭhamudrā), remains motionless. || 26 ||
Placing both hands on the ground, one should slowly strike the vital breath;
having drawn up both shanks, the wind vibrates rapidly.
The connection between Soma, Sūrya, and Agni arises for the sake of immortality;
from that, the state of death is produced, and therefore one should exhale the vital air (vāyu). || 28 ||

Having thoroughly practiced Mahāvedha, which bestows great accomplishment and destroys wrinkles, gray hair, and the piercing [of the vital centers], it is described by the most excellent practitioners. (29)
The three syllables are a great secret that destroys old age and death,
increases the digestive fire, and bestows the auspicious powers such as atomization (aṇimā).
And it is divided into eight parts, watch by watch, day after day; it generates a mass of merit and likewise shatters the flood of sins.
For those who possess the right training, the first practice is very brief; at the outset, one should observe the avoidance of fire, women, and the path.
Now, the Khecarī [mudrā].
One should gradually increase the practice through cutting, shaking, and milking, until the tongue touches the space between the eyebrows; this is Khecarī.
Success is attained when the tongue enters the cavity of the skull and moves in reverse;
with the gaze fixed between the eyebrows, this becomes the Khecarī Mudrā.
If one remains for half a moment, having turned away from the [lower] arts (kalā),
one is liberated in an instant from disease, old age, death, burden, and so forth. 35.
For him who knows the Khecarī-mudrā, there is neither disease nor death, neither sleep nor hunger or thirst, and no fainting shall occur. (36)
He who possesses the Khecarī-mudrā is not afflicted by disease, nor smeared by karma, nor bound by time. (37)
He whose mind moves in the void and whose tongue has gone to the void—by him this is known as Khecarī, which is saluted by the perfected ones (siddhas). (38)
He by whom the aperture above the uvula is sealed by the Khecarī-mudrā—his bindu does not leak, even when embraced by a passionate woman. (39)
Even when the drop has moved and reached the circle of the womb,
one should lead it upward by force through the power [of breath] while the womb is bound by the Yonimudrā.
The knower of yoga who, having made his tongue firm and directed it upwards, performs the drinking of the nectar (soma), undoubtedly conquers death within half a month. (41)
The poison does not spread within the body of that yogi who is constantly filled with the digits of the moon, even if he has been bitten by Takṣaka.
Just as fire does not leave the fuel, nor a lamp its oil and wick,
so the embodied soul does not abandon the body when it is filled with the digits of the moon.
The yogi should eat beef and drink the water of immortality;
him I consider to be of noble birth, while others are destroyers of their lineage.
The tongue is denoted by the word "go" (cow), and its entry into the palate is indeed the "eating of cow-meat"; that [act] is the destroyer of great sins. || 45 ||
Indeed, produced by the entry of the tongue and generated by fire,
that essence which flows from the moon is the nectar of the immortals.

Having forcefully restrained the tongue at the upper opening, one should contemplate the supreme Śakti within the cavity, as she flows from the vital breath onto the sixteen lotus-petals above. || 47 ||
The yogi, free from defects and with a body as tender as a lotus stalk, should drink the pure streams of nectar from the moving *lolakalā*; thus he lives for a long time. 48.
39b) If the tongue, which constantly drips with taste, should kiss the tip of the uvula— whether it be salty, pungent, sour, resembling milk, or like honey or clarified butter;

There shall be the removal of diseases, the overcoming of old age and death, the vomiting forth of knowledge from the scriptures, immortality endowed with the eightfold supernatural powers, and the summoning of hosts of perfected beings (siddhas). || 48 ||
This one seed has been created; there is but one mudrā, the Khecarī.
There is one God, the supportless; there is one state, the Manonmanī. (49)
That which enters the netherworld (pātāla) for a long time, and that which exists at the base of Mount Meru— the wise declare this to be the mouth of rivers; from that [mouth],
the moon-like essence flows from the body, and by that, death comes to men.
In that same way, one should bind the instrument; otherwise, there is no accomplishment of the body. || 50 ||
Now, the root-bonds (mūlabandha).
Pressing the perineum with the heel of the foot, one should contract firmly;
drawing the *apāna* upward is called the root-lock (*mūlabandha*).
By means of contraction, one forcibly causes the downward-moving *apāna* to go upward; yogis call this the "root-lock" (*mūlabandha*). (52)
Having firmly pressed the anus with the heel,
one should forcibly draw up the vital air (vāyu) so that the wind repeatedly moves upward.
When the prāṇa and apāna, along with the nāda and bindu, attain oneness through the mūlabandha,
there is no doubt that one proceeds to the perfect accomplishment of yoga.
Through the constant binding of the root, there is a union of the apāna and prāṇa breaths when urine and feces are diminished; thus, even an old man becomes young again.
When the apāna has moved halfway and the circle of fire has set forth,
then the long flame of the fire increases, struck by the wind.
Then, having gone to the fire, it draws the vital breaths from the hand;
by that, the fire residing within the body becomes intensely inflamed.
By that, the sleeping Kuṇḍalinī, being thoroughly heated, is awakened.
Struck by the staff, like a female serpent hissing, she would depart during her season. || 58 ||
When the vital wind has entered the *vila* (the opening), it moves within the *brahmanāḍī*; therefore, yogis should always constantly practice the binding of the root (*mūlabandha*). 59.
Now follows the binding of Oḍiyāna.
Because the vital breath (prāṇa) is increased within the Suṣumṇā and because it is bestowed [therein],
this [center] is therefore proclaimed by yogins as Uḍyāpāka.
Because the great bird (the vital breath) performs its flight there without rest, that indeed is called Uḍḍiyāṇa; therein the binding [of the breath] is prescribed.
One should perform this in the abdomen, above the navel and toward the lower end;
for this is the Uḍḍiyāṇa Bandha, the lion to the elephant of death.
Uḍḍiyāṇa is indeed the innate [bandha], as always taught by the Guru;
the yogi should practice it incessantly, and even an old man shall become young again. (63)
One should diligently perform the expansion [of the body] both above and below the navel;
by practicing this for six months, there is no doubt that one will overcome old age and death.
In the vajrāsana posture, one should firmly hold the feet with both hands near the region of the ankles; there, the trembling is suppressed.
One should cause [the breath] to enter the belly from the western end, then the heart, and then the throat,
very slowly, so that the vital breath does not reach the junction of the shoulders.
Indeed, among all the bandhas, Uḍḍiyāṇa is the supreme;
when the Uḍḍiyāṇa bandha is performed, liberation becomes natural.
Now follows the Jālāndhara-bandha.
Contracting the throat, one should firmly place the chin against the heart;
this is the bindu known as Jalandhara, considered the supreme death of death.
For it binds the network of vessels below and draws up water from the sky;
therefore, this "net-binding" posture destroys the flood of suffering in the throat. (69)
When the Jālandhara band, characterized by the constriction of the throat, is performed,
the nectar does not cook in the fire, nor does the vital breath (vāyu) rush upward.
By contracting the throat, one should firmly restrain the two channels;
this is to be known as the middle wheel, the binding of the sixteen supports.
These three excellent bonds, practiced by the great Siddhas, are known by the wise as the means of accomplishment for all Yoga Tantras and for yogins. (72)
By means of downward contraction and by the constriction of the throat,
[the breath] should be drawn into the central channel through the posterior extension, reaching from the aperture of the vital breath to the aperture of Brahma.
Having firmly contracted the root-seat (mūlasthāna), one should perform the Uḍḍiyāṇa lock;
having bound both the Iḍā and Piṅgalā, one should cause [the breath] to flow through the western path.
By this very method, one proceeds to the dissolution into the wind;
thereafter, neither birth nor death, nor old age, disease, and the like, occur.
Now, the definition of the contrary.
With the navel above and the sun above while the moon is below—this practice known as "the reversal" is obtained through the word of the Guru. (76)
For the practitioner who is constantly engaged in practice, abundant food should be provided in order to increase the digestive fire. 77.
In one who eats little food, the digestive fire arises in the body at that very moment;
on the first day, one should remain for a moment with the head downward and the feet upward.
One should practice for slightly more than a moment day after day;
within six months and a half, even wrinkles and gray hair are eliminated. (79)
He who practices this constantly for even a single watch (yāma) becomes a conqueror of time;
or else, [he masters] the vajrolī.
Even if one acts according to one's own will, without the restraints prescribed by Yoga, [the goal is not attained]. (80)
The yogi who knows through the *vajjoli* [practice] becomes a vessel for spiritual accomplishments;
in that regard, I consider two things to be difficult for anyone to obtain. (81)
Milk is the first [ingredient], and a woman who is submissive is the second;
one should practice the upward contraction (*ūrdhvakuñcana*) properly and gradually by means of these deluding [substances]. 82.
Whether a man or a woman, one who possesses the *vajrālī* [mantra] shall attain success;
with effort, by means of a net of arrows, one should blow upon the black-throated [Lord Śiva].
One should perform this very gradually for the sake of circulating the vital air (vāyu);
having drawn upward one's own bindu which has been made to revolve, one should preserve it.
Thus, by guarding the bindu, the knower of yoga conquers death;
death occurs through the falling of the bindu, while life arises from the retention of the bindu. 85.
The body of the yogi becomes fragrant through the retention of the *bindu*;
the body of the yogi becomes fragrant through the retention of the *bindu*. (86)
41a) As long as the semen remains stable in the body, from where can there be fear of death?
For the semen of men is dependent on the mind, and life is dependent on the semen. 86.
Therefore, one must protect both the semen and the mind with great effort;
likewise, a woman in her menses must protect her own discharge.
One should draw [the breath] upward by means of the perineum through the proper application of practice;
this yoga belongs to those who are meritorious, blessed, and endowed with the knowledge of reality. 88.
Success is attained by those free from envy, but not by those possessed of envy;
for the innate *uḷi*, the *śrāmara-uḷi*, and the *vajra-uḷi* arise only through awakening. 89.
Having cast ashes produced from burnt cow dung into water,
both the woman and the man should smear their own bodies above the *vajrīlī* and the *mehana*.
When two people are seated comfortably for a moment, having ceased all activity,
this is declared by yogis to be "natural salutation" (sahaja-añjali), always performed with faith.
This auspicious yoga bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; for a man who has properly mastered the skill of practice by contracting the *bindu*, it grants freedom even amidst enjoyments. 92.
If a woman, together with her consort, should protect her menstrual flow with a *vajrī* leaf, [she attains success]. || 93 ||
There is no doubt that her menses do not cease at all;
moreover, the sound within her body becomes known as the *bindu*. 94.
That *bindu* and that *rajas*, having become one within their own bodies through the practice of the yoga of *vajroli*, bring about all supernatural accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*). || 96 ||
One knows the past and the future, and the power of moving through the sky (khecarī) arises;
one attains the perfection of the body through the practice and yoga of vajrolī. || 96 ||
Therefore, this [yoga] bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon the practitioner;
for this reason, this yoga is accomplished only by those who possess merit. || 97 ||
Now, the activation of the power (śakti).
Kuṭilāṅgī, Kuṇḍalinī, Bhujaṅgī, Śakti, Īśvarī, Kuṇḍalī, and Arundhatī—these are indeed synonyms expressing the same meaning. (98)
Just as one might forcibly open a door with a key, so too does the yogi pierce the door of liberation by means of Kuṇḍalinī. (99)
41b) By whichever path one must go to the stainless Gate of Brahmā, that gate is covered by the mouth; the Supreme Goddess is fast asleep. 100.
Above the *kuṇḍa* is the Kuṇḍalinī Śakti, who has been coiled eightfold;
she bestows liberation upon the yogins who have been bound by the bondage of the *yantra*. (101)
The Kuṇḍalinī is curved in form and coiled like a serpent;
he by whom that Śakti is set in motion is liberated, of this there is no doubt. (102)
Between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, even a wretched widow performing penance might, by force, attain that supreme state of Viṣṇu. || 103 ||
Grasping the tail, one should wake the sleeping female serpent without fear;
having abandoned sleep, she rises straight up forcefully.

Now, for one seated on the left-hand seat, that serpent [vessel] should be produced from the sun at the present time of late afternoon for a duration of half a watch; having put on its garment and grasped it, it should be constantly rotated. 105.
Measuring one span (vitasti) in length and four finger-breadths (caturaṅgula) in width, soft and white—this is declared to be the characteristic of the best among desired things. (106)
One should perform the contraction of the sun (the solar channel) and then cause Kuṇḍalinī to move;
for such a person, even if situated within the wheel of death, whence can there be fear of death? (107)
The breath flowing through the right nostril, drawn out long and filled with lunar water, always nourishes the immortal body prior to the bell (the uvula).
At the time of death, as the body comes under the power of the expansive fire from the multitude of channels that burn it, it does not produce another body,
just like the trunk of a tree that has been cut down.
Having set the Kuṇḍalinī in motion, one should especially practice the bellows-breathing (bhastrī);
by such constant practice, Yama himself fears the self-controlled practitioner.
Likewise, through such practice, there are Sūryabheda, Ujjāyī, and also Śītalī; for one who is thus disciplined in practice, tranquil, and self-controlled, what [fear] can there be? (110)
For a period of two muhūrtas, due to being moved fearlessly,
this Kuṇḍalinī residing in the Suṣumṇā is drawn slightly upward.
By that [means], Kuṇḍalinī is raised up from that Suṣumnā;
therefore, this Prāṇa abandons it and proceeds spontaneously toward the Suṣumnā. || 112 ||
Therefore, one should constantly move the amaruṇḍatī within the womb of Śambhu;
for by moving it, the yogi is swiftly liberated from diseases.
The yogi by whom the power (śakti) has been set in motion becomes a vessel for spiritual accomplishments;
what is the use of much speaking on this matter? He conquers time with ease.
For one who observes the vow of celibacy and always eats wholesome and moderate food,
success is seen from the *maṇḍala* through the practice of yoga involving the *kuṇḍalinī*.
One should mix the lunar [substance] emerging from practice with the [elemental] power;
on its day, when placed on the head, it bestows divine vision.
Regarding the seventy-two thousand channels that are purified of impurities, what means of cleansing exists other than the practice of Kuṇḍalinī? (117)
Thus ends the movement of the power (śakti).
Thus, these ten mudrās have been proclaimed by the primordial Lord Śambhu;
indeed, even a single one among them is sufficient for the attainment of all siddhis. (118)
Without Rājayoga, the earth does not shine; without Rājayoga, the night does not shine; and without Rājayoga, even a manifold mudrā does not shine. (119)
One should practice all mental yoga for a month; the wise person should ensure that the activity of the mind does not wander elsewhere. 120.
Even the central channel, though obstructed, becomes entirely permeable for the yogi through firm practice by means of postures (āsana), breath control (prāṇasaṃyāma), and mudrās. || 121 ||
For those who remain sleepless during their practices while the samādhis have arisen within the mind, Rudrāṇī bestows the supreme mudrā, Bhadrā, and spiritual accomplishment (siddhi). || 122 ||
He who bestows the traditional instruction on the mudrās is indeed the true great guru, the master; he is the Lord himself in visible form. (123)
He who, being diligent, practices the supreme mudrā according to his word, becomes a defier of time through qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest. || 124 ||
Thus ends the third instruction, titled "The Characteristics of Mudrās," in the Haṭhapradīpikā composed by the lord of yogis, Svātmārāma, who is like a wish-fulfilling gem for his own self.
Salutations to the auspicious Guru, whose nature is the dissolution of sound (nāda) and the point (bindu);
he is the stainless state to which those who are ever devoted attain. 1.
The mind is the lord of the senses, but the wind is the lord of the mind;
the dissolution of the wind is its lord—I take refuge in that Lord. || 2 ||
With breath extinguished, movement destroyed, and the body dissolved;
motionless and free from all change—victory to the absorption (laya) of the yogis! || 3 ||
With all volitional constructions severed and all activity completely ceased, he remains conscious of his own state until the moon and stars exist; thus he lives.
Wherever there is vision, there is dissolution; for one who is detached from the elements and the senses, the Vedas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas are like common courtesans.
The Śāmbhavī Mudrā alone is like a secret, noble lady:
the gaze is fixed externally while the internal object is perceived, free from blinking or opening the eyes.
This is that Śāmbhavī Mudrā, which is praised in all Tantras.

When the yogi exists with his mind and breath dissolved within the internal object (the bindu), and he gazes with a steady, star-like eye, he should look neither outward nor downward; at that time, he should not see anything.
This indeed is the Khecarī Mudrā, which, when attained through the grace of the Guru, causes that Śāmbhava state— the reality which transcends both the void and the non-void— to manifest.
Even though she is capable, she is pierced upon being understood by Khecarī;
and once pierced, nectar flows from the Moon, which possesses a divine form.
The sun devours all of that, and by that, the physical body becomes subject to old age;
yet therein exists a divine instrument which acts as an adversary to the sun.
This is to be known through the instruction of the Guru, and not by means of millions of scriptural meanings;
therefore, disciples should serve the Guru with their whole being.

The glorious Ādinātha has proclaimed that there are one and a half crores of modes of absorption (laya); yet among these absorptions, the single practice of continuous contemplation on the Sound (nāda) is the most preeminent. 11.
Seated in the mukta posture, the yogi, having assumed the Śāmbhavī mudrā,
should with one-pointed mind listen to the internal sound within his right ear.
Fire produced from wood is extinguished along with the wood; the mind produced by sound is extinguished along with the sound. 43a) // 13 //
Having forgotten all musical instruments, the mind, like milk poured into water,
becomes one with the Sound and then dissolves into the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).
Through constant practice, the self-controlled one should become indifferent toward all else;
the realization of the Transmental state is immediately apprehended through the Sound alone. (15)
Having completely abandoned all thought and all activity at all times,
the mind dissolves into two ways through constant connection with the sound alone.
Just as there is the beginning and the potting [of clay], so too is the practice;
completion occurs in all yogas—these are the stages of yoga. (17)
At the Brahma-granthi, there occurs a piercing, a self-bliss born from the void;
at that very moment, a wondrous sound is heard everywhere throughout the body.
Possessing a divine body, self-luminous, with a divine fragrance and free from disease, when the heart is completely empty, the yogin’s undertaking shall take place. (19)
Now, the state of the jar.
Having fixed the breath in the second nāḍī, the wind becomes situated in the middle;
the yogi should remain firm in posture, for through knowledge alone he becomes equanimous. (20)
Then, from the bursting of the Viṣṇu-knot, there arises in the supreme void a sound like that of a mṛdaṅga drum or a kettledrum, which indicates supreme bliss.
Then, on the third [day], having become like the great roar of a lion, it enters the Great Void (mahāśūnya), which is the refuge of all accomplishments (siddhi). || 22 ||
Thus Cittānanda was born, originating from Sahajānanda;
he was devoid of pleasure and pain, old age and death, hunger and sleep. (23)
Then, having pierced the Rudra-knot, the wind (vital energy) moves through all the pressure-points;
this is the state of completion.
Upon its accomplishment, the sound arises with momentum like the resonance of a flute;
at that time, the mind becomes one with the element, designated as Rājayoga. || 24 ||
He becomes a creator and destroyer, equal to a lord of yogis;
whether [the power] exists on the left or not, the great [power] is broken within the body. 43b) 25.
The happiness consisting of liberation is obtained through the Rājayoga;
I consider those who, ignorant of the Rājayoga, rely solely on the practice of Haṭha, to be like servants or farmers who are deprived of fruit despite their exertion. (26)
Reality is the seed, Haṭha is the field, and equanimity is likewise the water;
the wish-fulfilling creeper of Unmanī will come into being immediately.
Rājayoga, samādhi, unmanī, and manonmanī;
immortality, non-duality, the supportless, and the stainless. || 28 ||
The state beyond the mind, the reality of the mind, the void of the void, the supreme state, liberation while living, the innate, and the fourth—these are indeed one in expression. (29)
Both of these, which I highly regard, are for the swift attainment of the Unmanifest:
the supreme reality, as well as the practice of Nāda-yoga. (29)
Abandoning all thoughts with a vigilant mind, one who desires the sovereignty of yoga should meditate solely upon the Sound (Nāda). 30.
Then, covering his ears with his fingers, the sage should fix his mind on whatever sound he hears at the base [of the ears], until it attains a state of stability. || 31 ||
As this sound (nāda) is being practiced, it veils external noise;
therein, at the first stage of practice, the sound is manifold and great.
Then, as that practice increases, it is heard in an increasingly subtle manner; wherever the mind first moves within the sound (nāda), [there it remains]. (33)
Remaining steady right there, one dissolves together with that [reality], wandering through the pleasure garden of rest for the intoxicated elephant-lord of the mind. (34)
When the sound has ceased and the sharp kusha grass is ready for the rite of leading [the victim], one must certainly not perform the blocking of the ears, mouth, eyes, or nose. || 35 ||
Regarding purification in the channel of Suṣumṇā, a clear and stainless discourse is heard:
having understood the junction of the Suṣumṇā and having brought the vital breath into the middle path. (36)
Having performed this, she should join it at the location of the moon within the aperture of the vital breath (prāṇaraṃdhra).
Thus is the statement of Vasiṣṭha. 36.
The moon and the sun move within the iḍā and the piṅgalā;
the moon is said to be tāmasa, while the sun is called rājasa. (37)
All methods of Haṭha and Laya Yoga are for the sake of attaining Rājayoga; a person who has ascended to Rājayoga transcends the five states of time.
Thus ends the fourth instruction in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*, a compendium of all scriptures composed by the lord of yogis, Svātmārāma.
Salutation to Śrī Rāma.
Salutation to the lotus-like Śrīmatkāmapīṭha.
Salutation to the Guru of Kāmapīṭha, the Great Rudra who is the destroyer of the three cities and the initiator into all mantra-initiations.
Now I shall correctly proclaim the Śāvarītantra as taught by Kāmākṣā-Śavarī,
which is exceedingly effective in producing immediate conviction.
Once, on the slopes of the Himalayas, while searching for Kārttikeya,
she assumed the form of a Śavarī woman, her mind filled with longing.
He questioned Śambhu, the Lord of all, who bestows the fruit of all the Āgamas.
Gaurī said:
O God, all the tantras— whether Paurāṇic, Vaidika, or others of incomparable power— exist upon the surface of the earth and even in the depths of the netherworld.
The yakṣa-mantras are quickly perfected; examine those of the piśācas as well.
Indeed, there are the yakṣiṇī-paṭalas, which move through the leaves and the solar rays.
Then there are the Traipuras, the Śaivas, the Cāṇḍas, the Cuvukas,
the Kaulas known as Bhillas, the Kairātas, and the Pathapañcis.
All the five-night festivals have been ordained;
those which are concealed, those which are directed toward the supreme, and even those which are the guardians of Dharma.
O Giriśa, even the hundreds of medicinal juices produced through mantras, yantras, and other means— all those are merely the products of perfected śabaras.
They bear fruit and do not bear fruit quickly; for that reason, they remain untrusted.
What is the cause of this, O Lord? Tell me that, and something else as well.
That which pertains to any living being whatsoever bears fruit immediately and swiftly upon the earth;
it is devoid of the authority of either the wise or even the knower of wisdom.
As soon as it is performed, let them bring forth fruit; for whatever has come to mind,
by that one attains the incomparable— there is no doubt in this regarding the perfected one.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and whoever else is born of other castes—
all these are qualified [for this practice], adorned by the immediate fruit [of its success].
Tell me this, O Mahādeva, ocean of hundreds of oceans of compassion;
through your grace, may I immediately attain that which is unsurpassed.
Śambhu said:
Well asked, O Great Goddess, regarding this secret of mantras and yantras;
though this should not be told to anyone, nevertheless, it shall be spoken before you.
O Bhavānī, O fair-faced one, listen to why you are my beloved:
in the past, I indeed churned all the Pañcatantras together.
Having rendered them essence-less with his hand, they no longer bore fruit here and there;
[he did this] by means of the one known as Siddha-Śāvara, who possessed the form of Vīrabhadra.
O Goddess, that which was composed by me as a burnt seed does not bear fruit for anyone; it was fashioned for the sake of delusion and serves only to increase the ranks of the heretics.
In this very place, the Kaula scriptures and others likewise bear fruit;
and by Dakṣa, in the guise of a rogue, the one known as the Śābara-siddha [was produced].
In the past, he employed [his power] and agitated the three worlds;
therefore, O Great Goddess, his power has been destroyed by me.
If a yogin abandons the object of practice, such as *hoḥ* or *hāḥ*,
then his [practice] will sometimes succeed, or else it will be corrupted by his own lack of qualification.
To you, the most worthy of honor, belongs this tantra which bestows all fruits;
it is named Kāmarūpa, and therein lies the increase of the desire-granting kalpa.
"O fair-faced one, when this is practiced by you as well,
it shall become the foremost among tantras, known as the Śavarī-tantra."
In this world, there are many mental states expressed through the languages of gods and humans,
as well as mental states expressed through the languages of yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas.
Furthermore, there are the languages arising from various regions, produced both in their natural and reverse orders;
likewise, there is the regulation of time and the determination of subtle time.
The rules regarding planetary conjunctions and the like, as well as the determination of medicinal prescriptions—these indeed are the primary matters here; the rule for meditation and such is not so.

(One should recite starting from the letter *A*, denoted by the word "right ear," up to the letter *Kṣa*, denoted by the word "left ear. Then, one should perform the rosary (*akṣamālā*) according to the method described in other texts, beginning with "again, in reverse order" and so forth.)
45a) That rite is not proclaimed for Nāpinya, nor is it established for Prāṇa;
nor is the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) performed externally— that is desired as the Mātṛkā-nyāsa.
O sinless one, you should perform the recitation according to the prescribed method for the rosary;
having performed meditation before the deity, [the recitation] should be from the right.
The letter following *ka* (i.e., *kha*) and so forth, with the *visarga*, together with the *bindu*, forms a letter of the Mātṛkā;

In a grove of orange and coconut trees, or on a riverbank during the night on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Mādhava; or else on a beautiful island adorned with such a forest; or else on the shore of a lotus-filled lake, a pond graced by *kuṭaja* trees and resplendent with *punnāga* and other such trees.

how was this Vidyā, so difficult for Dakṣa to propitiate, bestowed upon me by you?

while dwelling on Mount Nīla and subsisting on sacrificial offerings, she was propitiated by me.

yet even then, O compassionate one, you showed no mercy toward me in my youth.

Meditating upon her alone and chanting her name at all times,
he spent eight thousand excellent years in this manner.

Moreover, even if there were some favor toward her, it is not seen;
